extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of poetry/practical criticism; general readers learning how to read and judge poems
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reading, interpreting, and judging lyric poems in a practical-criticism classroom: focuses on how meter, diction, imagery, reader response, and tendencies in diction affect critical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance for a precise image released spontaneously
rubrics_metrics.description: The precise image let loose cannot of course be counted against the poet; the tendency towards the exaggerated and ludicrous might.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single vivid or odd image, if spontaneous, should not be condemned automatically; what matters is whether the tendency toward exaggeration or ludicrousness is a recurring feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of humour (or its absence) as a critical marker
rubrics_metrics.description: I could not help thinking that the poet who could leave the third verse as it stands lacks a sense of humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers may judge lines as faulty if they seem to lack a healthy sense of humour, but this is subjective and alternate readers may regard the same expression as one of the poem's perfections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony of thought, sound, and expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The dominant note of this poem is harmony of thought and sound and expression — and also of the atmosphere and the aspirations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether meter, rhythm, diction, and imagery work together to produce a unified effect; e.g., a sudden change of rhythm that perfectly expresses meaning is a strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter/rhythm matching the movement of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The rhythm seems to match the march of the thought perfectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the poet's metrical choices (including sudden rhythmic shifts) serve the thought or merely call attention to themselves; metre can be a test of whether a reader has understood what the poet is attempting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness/consistency of metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: If the fourth verse is not literally true, the metaphor is valueless. If it is true, the trees should not be in a lyric of faith, but in a Botanic Garden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether a figurative image is coherent within the poem; an implausible literal reading may render a metaphor ineffective unless the poet intends an imaginative rather than literal claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single fault versus tendency (pattern detection)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single fault, by itself, may always be merely clumsiness. To decide whether it is more than this we should have to consider with it such things as ... What may be just a blunder, taken by itself, becomes evidence of a tendency when it finds echoes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolate apparent errors and then look for echoes elsewhere in diction, manner, or imagery to determine whether they indicate a characteristic tendency of the poet or merely an isolated slip.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity/authenticity of feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The blend of religious experience with nature is forceful and sincere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether emotional or devotional expression seems genuinely felt and integrated with the poem's materials, rather than self-conscious or merely rhetorical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of smugness/self-conscious moralising
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost everywhere there is a certain smugness which makes it rather repellent... The desire expressed in the last verse... is much too self-conscious and far-fetched to make me regard it as good poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lines that read as moralizing, self-satisfied, or contrived may repel readers; look at diction and tone for signs of self-consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness/spontaneity vs. over-crafted facture
rubrics_metrics.description: Verse 4 also exhibits its facture, wears its craft on its sleeve... is discerned to be nastily 'forced'... Verse 5, Parable is served up cold... an infallible symptom of the anaesthetising of spontaneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise poems whose craft is unobtrusive and spontaneous; be suspicious of passages that display technique so openly they seem forced or contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to commercialised, stock 'uplift' or homiletic tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The gas that breeds above the staid and unspontaneous uplift spirit of a Democracy whose Literature has been commercialised... Parable is served up cold, as at Sunday Supper — the dose is almost domestically homiletic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for canned or commercialized sentimental tones (stock uplift) and homiletic parables presented without imaginative freshness; these are often judged negatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing poem-text from reader's private associations (stock responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The root question... is whether these responses reflect the poem itself, or some private poem prompted by the material set before the reader and by his own reminiscences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating responses, test whether praise or criticism arises from the text itself or from the reader's personal memories and conventional associations; avoid conflating the two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and unity of central idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity and unity seem to me the outstanding qualities of this poem. There is only one central idea: the bond between man and nature in mutual worship: Each verse is confined to this one idea, nothing is admitted to suggest any other train of thought...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poem that maintains a single central idea with each unit (verse/section) confined to it is often judged effective; note exceptions where variety is deliberately pursued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universalizing a private feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet has succeeded in universalizing his desire to worship... suggest the long aisle of a great cathedral... fill it with gladness and delight in a way that trebles the evocative power of its solemnity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a personal feeling is rendered in terms that reach a wider human experience (universalization) rather than remaining merely private or idiosyncratic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evocative power of imagery and epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The worshipping trees arise and run'... What a use of epithet and what a clear picture!... A very lovely poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality epithet and clear, evocative images that deepen the poem's effect are strengths; evaluate imagery for precision and emotional resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on textual detail rather than general feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the admirers were more occupied by the effect of the poem on their feelings than by the detail of the poem itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should attend to specific textual features (wording, rhythm, imagery) rather than relying solely on subjective feeling or overall mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of gross sentimentality/maudlin emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: If this... should prove not to be silly, maudlin, sentimental twaddle... Such it certainly seems to me, and I loathe it. It is a revelling in emotion for its own sake, that is nothing short of nauseating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether expressed emotion is supported by craft and insight rather than being merely self-indulgent or mawkish; consider both content and versification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and fitness of diction (word-choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: I object to 'cosy,' and 'tingling' used of a piano that elsewhere 'booms' or is 'appasionato' is just absurd... 'piano' as a disyllabic has an unpleasant sound. 'The heart of me' is also obnoxious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine precise word choices for semantic fit, register, and sonic fitness; mismatched or awkward diction can derail a poem's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close reading: noticing exact words and contrasts
rubrics_metrics.description: It is illuminating to compare the type of comment with the closeness of reading evinced... 8.13 has not noticed any difference between 'tingling' and 'tinkling'... He has not even observed which word is used when.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good criticism requires attention to exact wording, contrasts, and small textual details (including variant words and their placement); careless summary reading ('newspaper' type) misses essential clues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge and correct treatment of referenced arts (e.g., music)
rubrics_metrics.description: As to the sounds emitted by pianos, a point of fact that proved as disastrous to many readers... Since I have formed my own opinion on the poem, I have experimented... each has started to grin when we have arrived at the phrase 'a child sitting under a piano, in the boom of the tingling strings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a poem invokes another art (music, architecture, etc.), check whether the references are plausible and whether readers need acquaintance with the art to assess the image; incorrect factual objections can betray inattention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre and verse-form technicalities matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The metre, however, detracts considerably from the poem... It is line 3 that spoils the verse... 'sitting under the piano' upsets the whole balance of the metre... the splitting-up of 'cast down' over two lines is inexcusable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess lineation, beat counts, enjambment, and how words are split across lines; metrical misfits can injure a poem's movement and intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of importing conventional movement or feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: All the difficulties of the stock emotional response are paralleled in the stock reading of metre. It is as easy to import a conventional movement into the rhythm as to drag in conventional feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers often unconsciously impose familiar rhythms or sentiments on a poem; critics should attempt to hear and read the poem on its own terms rather than superimposing stock patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poem may require imaginative closeness to be understood
rubrics_metrics.description: Perhaps if someone had read the poem to him, giving decent prominence to the natural speech rhythm, he would have been converted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider reading the poem aloud or imagining its speech-rhythm; some metrical effects are only evident when the poem's natural cadence is apprehended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'appeals to the gallery' and hackneyed phraseology
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot help disliking the evocative use of such phrases as 'old Sunday evenings,' 'cosy parlour,' 'vista of years,' etc., which are nothing but so many calls to one's loose emotion to attach itself to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of conventional sentimental phrases intended merely to trigger ready emotional responses; originality and fresh phrasing are preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance judgement—sincerity need not guarantee perfection; craft may mask insincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Carelessness may accompany the sincerest feelings... Deft craftsmanship can easily elude this too convenient test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce value judgments to a single test (e.g., 'sincerity' = good). Consider multiple factors: craftsmanship can make insincere material persuasive, and sincere feeling can exist alongside technical lapses.
